chef_bio.origin: Nara — within Nara Park, beside Todaiji Nigatsudo.
chef_bio.background: 龍美堂 sits directly south of Todaiji's Nigatsudo Hall, famous for the Omizutori fire-and-water rites, and has long served as a resting spot for pilgrims. The shop pours tea boiled in an iron kettle said to be over 200 years old and offers a sweeping view over Nigatsudo and the Nara Basin. It also displays rare items connected to Nigatsudo and the Omizutori ceremony.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop is the officially permitted maker of Gyoho miso, the secret-recipe miso said to have been used by the ascetic monks who shut themselves away during Nigatsudo's rites to build their spiritual strength — a practice the temple traces back over a thousand years to the priest Jitchu, disciple of Todaiji's founding abbot Roben.
chef_bio.specialty: Handmade warabi mochi generously dusted with freshly-ground kinako (soybean flour), and large old-fashioned ohagi made with the shop's own homemade red-bean paste. The shop is also the licensed maker of 行法味噌 (Gyoho miso), sold as a souvenir; in summer it serves shaved ice with house anko.

anecdotes.text: 二月堂と奈良盆地を望む抜群のロケーションで、龍美堂自慢の甘味をご賞味下さい。
この行法は天平の昔、東大寺開山良辧僧正の高弟實忠和尚によって創められましてから今日まで千何百年の間一度も途絶えたことのないあらたかな秘法でございます。

positives.text: Signature warabi mochi is made from bracken starch and kinako rather than wheat flour, and ohagi is glutinous rice with red-bean paste — base recipes that typically contain no wheat and no animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A quiet, traditional temple-side tea house where pointing at the warabi-mochi and ohagi display works fine, but there is no English menu or allergen support, so a foreign student with dietary needs should arrive with a guide or translated phrases.

nara_cafe_tamaki.gf_detail: This is a traditional kissaten whose mainstays are coffee, toast, cake, and homestyle dishes — all wheat-heavy and prepared in a shared kitchen with no gluten-free accommodation documented. Not suitable for celiacs.
nara_cafe_tamaki.vegan_detail: No vegan offering is documented. Black hand-roasted coffee is the safest plant-based option, but food items (toast, cake, pudding, homestyle cooking) typically contain dairy, eggs, or animal stock. Vegans would need to ask, and options will be very limited.
nara_cafe_tamaki.notes: [Mom & Pop] One of the oldest coffee houses in Nara — by the proprietor's own account effectively the oldest still standing, as the two that preceded it have closed. chef_bio.background: One of the oldest coffee houses in Nara — by the proprietor's own account effectively the oldest still standing, as the two that preceded it have closed. It sits on a narrow lane heading into the historic Naramachi quarter, in a quiet wood-toned space behind a white-and-black exterior.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner insists the place is a 'cafe' rather than a kissaten, partly because a cafe may serve alcohol — and indeed many regulars drop in to sip spirits cut with their own preferred ratio of water alongside small snacks.
chef_bio.specialty: Hand-roasted coffee made by a roasting method handed down from the founder, alongside homestyle cooking and toast; in earlier years the shop was loved for its bittersweet homemade pudding and a notably spicy house curry.

anecdotes.text: The energetic proprietor greets guests together with the shop dog, Kuma, and her warm chatter is regarded as one of the real pleasures of a visit.
After her husband passed away, the menu drifted away from its old signature items toward the homestyle dishes she now cooks herself.
The coffee follows a roasting style preserved from the shop's first-generation owner.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A traditional coffee house centered on toast, cake, and homestyle dishes in a single shared kitchen; cross-contact with wheat is effectively unavoidable and no gluten-free handling is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: No vegan menu is documented; food items generally rely on dairy, eggs, or animal-based stock, so dedicated vegan preparation is not indicated.

positives.text: Plain black hand-roasted coffee is available and is the most reliably plant-based item on offer.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, owner-run old-school coffee house where the chatty proprietor speaks Japanese; basic Japanese or a translation app will make the visit far smoother and more enjoyable.

nara_kasho_senjuan_yoshimune_.gf_detail: The house specialty is warabimochi, traditionally a wheat-free confection. The standard version blends sweet potato starch with domestic bracken (warabi) starch; the premium "pure" warabimochi (純本生わらび餅) uses 100% domestic bracken starch with only sugar and water. So the core sweet contains no wheat. However, it is dusted with kinako (roasted soybean flour) and the shop publishes no gluten-free or cross-contamination guarantees, and other wagashi sold here may contain wheat. Celiacs should ask directly before eating.
nara_kasho_senjuan_yoshimune_.vegan_detail: The signature warabimochi is plant-based: bracken/sweet-potato starch, sugar, water, and kinako (soybean flour) topping, with no animal products in its core recipe. This is a confectionery shop, not a vegan-focused destination, and ingredient lists vary by item (some wagashi may use eggs or dairy). No formal vegan menu or cross-contact policy is documented, so vegans should confirm individual items.
nara_kasho_senjuan_yoshimune_.hours_raw: Retail 10:00-18:00 (closed only on New Year's Day). The tea room 'Senju Saryo' operates mainly on weekends and holidays, around 13:00-17:00, serving only warabimochi and drinks (shaved ice is not offered at the main shop; it is available seasonally at the Nakamachi branch).

chef_bio.background: Founded in 1936 (Showa 11) by Yamamoto Yoshio, who first learned the confectioner's craft through an uncle's candy business in the early Showa years. After the war the workshop made candies under the name Sanwa Seika, then evolved into traditional wagashi. The second generation, Yamamoto Kenji, grew the business, and since 1998 the third generation, Yamamoto Tetsuya, has led the shop, now in its ninth decade in Nara.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop aims to create sweets, spaces, and hospitality that make the heart quietly calm — what they call 'おだやかな幸せ' (calm happiness).
chef_bio.specialty: Fresh warabimochi (生わらび餅) — a melt-in-the-mouth bracken-starch sweet dusted with kinako. The standard version blends domestic bracken starch with sweet-potato starch; the top-grade 純本生わらび餅 uses 100% domestic bracken starch with only sugar and water, hand-kneaded by veteran artisans. A historic candy called 古代瓦 (ancient roof tile) is named for the imagery of Todaiji and Nara's old architecture.

anecdotes.text: The shop's warabimochi was recognized with the Prime Minister's Award at the 21st National Confectionery Exposition, the result of extensive research into classical texts to recreate an additive-free, naturally soft sweet.

On weekends and holidays a small tea space, 千壽茶寮, opens in the afternoon serving the fresh warabimochi with a drink; in summer the warabimochi also appears in a fluffy Japanese-style shaved ice at the company's Nakamachi shop.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The shop is a general wagashi confectionery that also sells wheat-containing sweets; no gluten-free production line or cross-contamination policy is published, so shared utensils/surfaces are likely.

staff_allergy_handling.text: No published allergen or staff allergy-handling protocol; commentary on warabimochi allergens recommends contacting the maker directly to confirm ingredients.

positives.text: The premium warabimochi is made from only domestic bracken starch, sugar, and water — no additives — and the core warabimochi recipe contains no wheat, making it a relatively simple, plant-based sweet (note the kinako topping is soy).

cultural_comfort.note: A welcoming, walk-in-friendly old confectionery shop where you can point at the famous warabimochi and pay easily; a few words of Japanese and a smile go a long way, but no special skills are needed to buy or enjoy a sweet here.

nara_junkissa_shinroku_x_oshi.gf_detail: This is a donut-and-coffee kissaten. The signature items are hand-made fried donuts, which are wheat-based, and there is no indication of any gluten-free menu, dedicated equipment, or allergy accommodation. Not suitable for celiac or strict gluten-free diners.
nara_junkissa_shinroku_x_oshi.vegan_detail: The core offering is fried wheat donuts (typically made with egg, dairy and butter) and coffee. No vegan menu or plant-based options are documented, and the parfait/coffee drinks would normally use dairy. Not a vegan destination.

chef_bio.origin: Nara (Kitamachi), built on the site of the former neighborhood cafe Kissaten Mickey
chef_bio.background: A small, calm retro coffee shop in Nara's Kitamachi district, just north of the central station area near Hannya-ji temple. It opened on November 24, 2025, in the space formerly occupied by 'Kissaten Mickey,' a cafe long loved by the local community, and was reborn as a collaboration between the Shinroku kissaten concept and Tokyo-based OSHIMA DONUTS. The interior keeps a nostalgic Showa-era calm while pairing it with a modern donut counter.
chef_bio.philosophy: A place where 'nostalgic and new' are meant to live together in harmony, welcoming families, children and neighbors as a casual everyday gathering spot rather than a high-end establishment.
chef_bio.specialty: Hand-made fluffy fried donuts (nine varieties, with the standard Oshima Donut a favorite) and hot coffee, plus a here-only original creation, the Shinjika ('sacred deer') Donut Parfait. Coffee is offered at a discount when bought as a donut set.

anecdotes.text: The shop took over the premises of the beloved old neighborhood cafe 'Kissaten Mickey,' reopening as 'Junkissa Shinroku x Oshima Donut Nara' on November 24, 2025, blending the old retro charm with hand-made donuts from a Tokyo donut maker.
An original menu item found nowhere else, the 'Shinjika Donut Parfait' (named for Nara's sacred deer), is served alongside the signature 290-yen fluffy fried donuts.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The shop fries wheat-based donuts on site; no gluten-free menu or dedicated equipment is documented, so cross-contamination should be assumed.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed, family-friendly neighborhood coffee shop where a friendly greeting and pointing at the donut display will get you by, though staff likely speak limited English.

nara_tsuruya_tokuman_nara_san.gf_detail: This is a traditional Japanese-sweets maker. Its core products are wheat-based: the signature 三笠 (mikasa / dorayaki) is made with wheat flour, eggs and honey, and other baked confections similarly use flour. There is no documented gluten-free menu, no allergen labeling for celiacs, and no separate preparation. Not suitable for those requiring strict gluten-free.
nara_tsuruya_tokuman_nara_san.vegan_detail: As a wagashi shop, some items are plant-based by tradition — e.g. red-bean-paste sweets and the kakigori topped with wasanbon syrup, kuromitsu (black sugar syrup) and kinako (soybean flour) over shaved ice and bean paste contain no animal products in their basic form. However, signature baked items like the 三笠/dorayaki and 上生菓子 contain eggs (and the dorayaki contains honey), and there is no vegan labeling or guarantee. A vegan should ask item-by-item; pure adzuki/kanten/kuromitsu/kinako sweets are the safer choices.
nara_tsuruya_tokuman_nara_san.hours_raw: Official site (Sanjo branch): 10:00-18:00, closed Mondays. Tabelog lists 09:00-18:00.
nara_tsuruya_tokuman_nara_san.notes: Tsuruya Tokuman is one of Nara's long-established wagashi (traditional Japanese confectionery) houses, founded in 1898 (Meiji 31) after branching off from the older Tsuruya Hachiman lineage, with a confectionery tradition the house describes as spanning well over a century. chef_bio.background: Tsuruya Tokuman is one of Nara's long-established wagashi (traditional Japanese confectionery) houses, founded in 1898 (Meiji 31) and associated with the older Nara Tsuruya (Tsuruya Hachiman) confectionery lineage, with a craft tradition the house describes as spanning well over a century. The shop sits on the old Mochiidono / Sanjo arcade streets in the heart of Nara, between Kintetsu Nara and JR Nara stations.
chef_bio.philosophy: The house emphasizes traditional methods and Nara's regional confectionery heritage, taking pride in long-standing craft; its mikasa has been presented to the imperial household on multiple occasions, commemorated by a thank-you plaque from Kashihara Shrine displayed in the shop.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature product is the 三笠 (mikasa) — a generous dorayaki-style pancake about 13cm across, made with large premium adzuki beans and a moist, fluffy batter, with a celebrated 'kenjo mikasa' version. The house also makes 上生菓子 (seasonal fresh sweets) and, in summer, an 'an-gori' shaved ice built on fluffy, slow-melting ice with secret house-made bean paste and generous wasanbon sugar syrup (dark-looking but wasanbon rather than kuromitsu), served with hot tea.

anecdotes.text: The flagship mikasa is named for Mt. Wakakusa, whose grass-covered slopes look like three stacked hats, and it is baked to stay fresh for about a week.

The main shop's eat-in cafe was renovated while preserving vintage elements — repurposing old wooden storage boxes (banju) as counter decor and historic sliding doors as table tops under a skylight-lit, deep-narrow room — often watched over by an energetic octogenarian proprietress, a former Japanese-dance practitioner whose performance fans are displayed as decor.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Company site confirms founding in Meiji 31 (1898) in Shimogozen-cho and three shops; a wagashi note article and nara-jisya.info confirm the 13cm kenjo mikasa, ~1-week freshness, Mt. Wakakusa naming, imperial presentations, the banju/sliding-door cafe renovation, and the wasanbon an-gori shaved ice.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A wheat-flour environment: baked goods such as dorayaki/mikasa are made with wheat flour on-site, so flour is present and cross-contact with any flour-free items cannot be ruled out.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Eggs and honey are used in the signature dorayaki/mikasa and the premises also handle bean-paste-only and kuromitsu/kinako sweets; shared utensils and surfaces mean cross-contact between egg-containing and plant-based items is plausible. No vegan separation is documented.

positives.text: Several items are inherently plant-based by tradition (adzuki bean paste, kanten, kuromitsu black-sugar syrup, kinako soybean flour over shaved ice), giving vegans some workable choices if they confirm ingredients per item.

cultural_comfort.note: A welcoming, casual neighborhood sweets shop where you can point at what you want; staff are unlikely to speak much English, so a translation app or pointing is your best bet, but a confectionery purchase is low-pressure for a first-timer.

nara_azekuraya.gf_detail: Not gluten-free safe. The core menu is wheat-based (udon, somen/nyumen, soba blends, mitarashi dango) and broths use bonito-and-kombu dashi; mitarashi sauce and tare are typically wheat-soy-sauce based. No gluten-free accommodation is documented.
nara_azekuraya.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The signature noodle and porridge sets use fish (bonito) dashi and include items like herring (nishin) and chicken donburi; sweets are plant-based but the kitchen is built around fish-stock broths. No vegan menu is documented.
nara_azekuraya.hours_raw: 11:00-15:00 (Tabelog lists 11:00-14:30); during Omizutori (Mar 1-14) approx 12:00-18:00. Closes when sold out.
nara_azekuraya.notes: [Mom & Pop] Azekuraya is a teahouse and sweets shop that traces its founding to the Edo period, tucked within Nara Park on the grounds near Todai-ji and Nigatsudo. Marked by a deer-motif noren curtain, it serves as a rest stop for visitors exploring the ancient capital.

chef_bio.background: Azekuraya is a teahouse and sweets shop that traces its founding to the Edo period, on the grounds of Nara Park within the Todai-ji precinct, with Nigatsudo close by. Marked by a deer-motif noren curtain, it serves as a rest stop for visitors exploring the ancient capital.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop describes itself as offering seasonal handmade cooking in simple vessels, a place to pause during sightseeing and take in the atmosphere of old Nara.
chef_bio.specialty: Yamato tea rice porridge (chagayu) sets, freshly grilled handmade mitarashi dango, homemade warabi mochi, and Rokusai (six-color) udon and noodle (nyumen) sets in a Kansai-style broth.

anecdotes.text: The shop is known for freshly grilled handmade mitarashi dango and self-made warabi mochi, with a chagayu (tea porridge) set presented as a gentle, traditional local Nara dish served with side dishes and pickles.
During the Omizutori festival (March 1-14) at Nigatsudo, the shop shifts from its usual 11:00-14:30 daytime schedule to special afternoon-into-evening hours of roughly 12:00-18:00.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Official site confirms Edo-period founding, the Zoshi-cho/Todai-ji-grounds location with Nigatsudo nearby, the deer noren, and the chagayu/dango/warabi-mochi/Rokusai-udon menu; Tabelog confirms the special Omizutori hours (~12:00-18:00).

gf_cross_contamination.text: Menu is heavily wheat-based (udon, nyumen/somen, soba, dango) prepared in a shared kitchen, so cross-contact with gluten is effectively unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Mitarashi dango sauce and noodle tare are typically based on wheat-containing soy sauce; no wheat-free soy sauce is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Noodle and porridge sets use bonito (fish) dashi broth, and the menu includes herring and chicken dishes, so plant-based sweets share a fish-stock kitchen.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual traditional teahouse popular with sightseers near Todai-ji; staff likely speak limited English, so a few basic Japanese phrases or pointing at the menu will help.

nara_poku_poku.gf_detail: This is a tonkatsu (breaded, deep-fried pork cutlet) specialist. The signature dish is coated in wheat-flour panko breadcrumbs and is not gluten-free. The accompanying vegetable soup and seasoned sides typically rely on standard dashi and seasonings, and the set rice is blended with barley (a gluten grain). There is no documented gluten-free menu or celiac-safe preparation, and no dedicated fryer. Not suitable for celiacs.
nara_poku_poku.vegan_detail: A pork specialty restaurant built entirely around Yamato Pork cutlets, ginger-grilled pork, pork steak, and katsu curry. While the meal includes a notably generous amount of vegetables (a heaping plate of cabbage and a vegetable-rich soup), the soup contains imitation crab and the dishes are not prepared as vegan/vegetarian. No plant-based main is documented. Not suitable for vegans.
nara_poku_poku.hours_raw: 11:15-14:30 (L.O. 13:30), 17:30-20:00 (L.O. 19:00). Closed Tuesdays, Fridays, the first Monday of the month, plus irregular closures. Reservation phone hours: 10:00-11:00, 15:00-17:00, 20:00-21:30.
nara_poku_poku.notes: [Mom & Pop] Chef Tsuyoshi Akeboshi trained at established Japanese restaurants and well-regarded hotels before opening this small shop in the historic Naramachi district in 2011. He runs it together with his wife as an intimate, reservation-only counter-and-tables eatery.

chef_bio.background: Chef Tsuyoshi Akeboshi trained at established Japanese restaurants and well-regarded hotels before opening this small shop in the historic Naramachi district in 2011. He runs it together with his wife as an intimate, reservation-only counter-and-tables eatery of about 12 seats.
chef_bio.philosophy: A health-minded, ingredient-first approach: the finest Yamato Pork cooked gently to highlight its natural sweetness, balanced by an abundance of vegetables and digestive teas before and after the meal.
chef_bio.specialty: Tonkatsu made from Yamato Pork (a premium Nara-prefecture brand pork prized for tender meat and sweet, oleic-acid-rich fat). The pork is coated in coarse panko for a light, crisp finish and fried gently in soybean oil at a low temperature (around 160C). It is served not with sauce but with Guerande sea salt from France blended with sweet tea, herbs, and the shop's own spices. Sets come with a heaping plate of cabbage, a vegetable-laden soup, a seasoned side, and rice blended with barley, Job's tears, and legumes; the meal opens with mekabu tea and closes with black oolong tea.

anecdotes.text: The shop is so small and the cooking so deliberate that it operates entirely by reservation, with weekend seats often filling up about a month in advance.
Rather than the usual tonkatsu sauce, diners are given Guerande sea salt blended with sweet tea and spices to draw out the pork's flavor.
Even the cabbage and vegetable soup alone are filling, reflecting the deliberately health-conscious composition of the set meals.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Serai.jp confirms chef Tsuyoshi Akeboshi (48), the 2011 opening, Yamato Pork, coarse panko, ~160C soybean-oil frying for ~3 minutes, the Guerande-salt-with-sweet-tea seasoning in place of sauce, and reservation-only seating for 12; naralunch corroborates the mekabu/black-oolong service and month-ahead weekend bookings.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The signature dish is wheat-panko-breaded deep-fried pork; the set rice is blended with barley, both gluten sources, so the meal is not gluten-free.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No allergen or soy-sauce ingredient information is documented; standard Japanese seasonings (typically wheat-containing soy sauce) should be assumed.

vegan_cross_contact.text: This is a pork specialty restaurant; even the vegetable soup contains imitation crab and no vegan main is offered.

positives.text: The pork is fried in soybean oil at a low temperature, and meals come with a notably generous amount of vegetables and digestive teas.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a tiny, completely reservation-only husband-and-wife shop where you should phone ahead in Japanese and arrive on time, so it is most comfortable for a student who can manage some basic Japanese or bring a Japanese-speaking friend.

nara_ashura.gf_detail: Not gluten-free or celiac-safe. A signature dish is "gluten curry" made with seitan (wheat gluten, グルテン, made from flour to mimic chicken), and the menu includes other wheat items (scones, omurice, spaghetti, papad). Despite the word "gluten-free" appearing in some third-party listing snippets, the kitchen actively uses wheat gluten and is not safe for celiacs.
nara_ashura.vegan_detail: Vegetarian establishment using no meat or fish. Many dishes are genuinely vegan (the bean/onion-based curries use no animal products, and dishes without egg, milk, or yogurt are available on request). However, it is not fully vegan: the spicy curry sauce can include yogurt (dairy) for sweetness/tang, and omurice/omelette dishes use eggs. Vegans should specifically ask for egg-, milk-, and yogurt-free preparations, which the kitchen accommodates.
nara_ashura.hours_raw: 12:00-20:30 (Mon, Tue, Sat, Sun); some sources list 12:00-20:00. Closed Wed, Thu, Fri. May close early when dishes sell out.
nara_ashura.notes: あしゅーら occupies a roughly 100-year-old machiya (traditional townhouse) tucked into the quiet southern edge of Naramachi, near Kyobate. chef_bio.background: あしゅーら occupies a roughly 100-year-old machiya (traditional townhouse) tucked into the quiet southern edge of Naramachi, near Kyobate. The old wooden interior is dressed with Indian and Asian crafts and a faintly temple-like, oriental atmosphere, giving the room the feel of a hideaway rather than a busy cafe.
chef_bio.philosophy: A meat- and fish-free kitchen built on organic, pesticide-free vegetables and brown rice. The mood is deliberately unhurried — guests summon the easygoing owner by ringing a bell or tapping a wooden fish block, and are even told they are welcome to doze off after eating.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature plate is a brown-rice (genmai) vegetable curry. The Calcutta-style sauce gets its depth from pesticide-free onions caramelized slowly and beans blended smooth, so it tastes rich without any meat or fish. A popular variation adds 'gluten' (seitan made from wheat flour) that is crisped up to mimic chicken. Other regulars include tofu croquettes, omurice, soup spaghetti, papad, plus a tea menu with chai and fresh carrot juice and house-baked scones.

anecdotes.text: Guests call the relaxed proprietor not by raising a hand but by ringing a small bell or striking a wooden fish block (mokugyo), and the cafe openly invites diners to take a nap after their meal.
The curry's signature 'gluten' is made from wheat flour and fried until crisp so that it tastes and bites like chicken despite being entirely plant-based.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Nara-gourmet confirms the century-old machiya organic/vegetarian cafe, the pesticide-free-onion-and-blended-bean brown-rice curry (Calcutta-style, balanced with yogurt), the crisped wheat 'gluten' seitan that mimics chicken, bell/wooden-fish summoning, and the nap invitation.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat gluten (seitan) is a core menu ingredient prepared in the same kitchen, so cross-contact with gluten is unavoidable; the venue is not suitable for celiacs.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Yogurt (dairy) is used in the spicy curry sauce and eggs are used in omurice/omelette dishes, so vegans must request egg-, milk-, and yogurt-free preparations.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Staff are described as friendly and happy to explain the food, and dishes made without egg, milk, or yogurt are available on request.

positives.text: Fully meat- and fish-free kitchen using organic, pesticide-free vegetables and brown rice, with many naturally vegan curry options.
English-language menu and barrier-free accommodations (braille menu, guide dogs welcome) make ordering and asking about ingredients easier for foreign visitors.

cultural_comfort.note: An English menu (and even a braille menu) is available and guide dogs are welcome, so a foreign student can order comfortably and ask about egg-, dairy-, or wheat-free options.

nara_cafe_oasis.gf_detail: No gluten-free offering is documented. The menu is built around wheat-based dishes — wood-fired pizza and pasta dominate — so this is not a celiac-safe destination and there is no indication of dedicated equipment or allergen handling.
nara_cafe_oasis.vegan_detail: No vegan options are documented. Signature dishes center on beef, chicken, sausage, sea urchin (uni) cream, cheese pizzas and dairy, with no stated plant-based menu. A vegan traveler should not rely on this place without contacting the cafe directly.
nara_cafe_oasis.hours_raw: Wednesday-Sunday and holidays 11:30-21:00 (last food order 20:30); closed Monday and Tuesday. Modeled here as 11:30-20:30 service window per the kitchen last-order time.
nara_cafe_oasis.notes: A café tucked into the Konishi Sakura-dori shopping arcade just a couple of minutes from Kintetsu Nara Station. chef_bio.background: A café on Konishi-cho (the Sakura-dori arcade area) just a couple of minutes from Kintetsu Nara Station. Despite sitting in the middle of town, the interior leans into a warm, resort-like feel with abundant wood and greenery, built around a wood-fired oven that sits in open view of diners.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen showcases live wood-fired cooking behind glass, aiming for a relaxed, welcoming spot that works from lunch through an evening drink.
chef_bio.specialty: Wood-fired cooking: stone-oven pizzas such as butter-chicken-curry pizza and quattro formaggi, a range of pasta including a seared-uni cream pasta, and heartier plates like wood-oven-finished Joshu beef (ichibo) roast beef with grilled vegetables. Lunch sets come with a choice of salad and dessert.

anecdotes.text: The head chef trained at a popular Western (yoshoku/Italian-style) restaurant, which the cafe credits for its hearty, full-flavored plates.
The wood-fired oven is the centerpiece of the room, with cooking visible through glass for a 'live' dining feel.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official gourmet-navi page and narakko confirm the Konishi-cho location near Kintetsu Nara, the glass-fronted wood-fired oven, a chef trained at a popular Western restaurant, the Joshu-beef ichibo roast beef, seared-uni cream pasta, butter-chicken-curry and quattro-formaggi stone-oven pizzas, and salad/dessert lunch sets.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed, spacious wood-and-greenery café where a foreign student can comfortably order pizza or pasta with a few words of Japanese and a pointed menu, though staff English may be limited.

nara_nishimura_tei.gf_detail: No documented gluten-free program. The café centers on rice-based dishes (hojicha-cooked rice, miso soup, seasonal small plates, Nara pickles), and a homestyle rice meal can be relatively low in obvious wheat, but miso, Nara pickles (often soy/koji-based), and any soy seasoning may contain wheat, and there is no stated celiac/cross-contamination protocol. Galettes and breads on the menu contain gluten. A celiac traveler must ask directly (info@nishimuratei.com / SNS) before relying on it.
nara_nishimura_tei.vegan_detail: Vegetarian and vegan diners can be accommodated for the signature tea-rice set (chameshi-zen): hojicha-cooked rice, miso soup, seasonal vegetable small dishes, and Nara pickles, served without the optional egg ('okan no tamagoyaki' is a paid add-on). Accommodation is documented in travel coverage; because dashi and miso choices are not specified online, a strict vegan should confirm the broth and seasonings (no fish dashi/bonito) when ordering or reserving.
nara_nishimura_tei.hours_raw: Café 11:00–17:00; closed Thursdays. (Lodging check-in 14:00–20:00, check-out by 10:00.) Hours may vary — check SNS.
nara_nishimura_tei.notes: [Mom & Pop] Nishimura-tei occupies a Nara machiya (traditional wooden townhouse) more than 100 years old that opened to the public in autumn 2019. chef_bio.background: Nishimura-tei occupies a Nara machiya (traditional wooden townhouse) more than 100 years old that opened to the public in autumn 2019. The owner, Sugimoto Yuta, graduated from university in Tokyo and worked at a graphic-design company and then in food-service before returning to his hometown and renovating the family house — his grandmother's home — keeping the original stairs, beams, and two gardens, into a guesthouse with a small café and rental space at the quiet southern edge of Naramachi.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen aims for food you could eat every day without tiring of it — gentle on the body and quietly nostalgic, evoking the comfort of a grandmother's home. The whole place is built around an 'obāchan-chi' (grandmother's house) feeling of unhurried rest.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature dish is the 'everyday tea-rice set' (毎日の茶飯膳): rice cooked with local Nara hojicha roasted tea, miso soup, seasonal vegetable small dishes, and Nara pickles (also offered vegetarian/vegan), with an optional homemade rolled egg ('okan no tamagoyaki') as an add-on. The café also serves coffee, tea, and sweets sourced from local Nara shops, plus seasonal items like a winter hibachi (charcoal-brazier) service with toasted handmade bread and mochi.

anecdotes.text: The building was the owner's own family townhouse — his grandmother's home — restored rather than rebuilt, so guests sit among the original stairs, beams, and two small gardens recreated as they once were.
A 'book-trade coffee' idea lets visitors swap a book recommendation for a coffee, reflecting the relaxed, conversational spirit of the house.
Sitting at the south end of Naramachi, between the JR Nara station area to the west and Kintetsu Nara station to the north, it's pitched as a calm rest stop for people walking the old town.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Rurubu confirms owner Sugimoto Yuta's Tokyo graphic-design-then-food-service career, his return to restore his grandmother's 100+yr machiya, and the two preserved gardens/stairs/beams; the READYFOR project and a web search confirm the autumn-2019 opening and the 880-yen hojicha 茶飯膳 (vegetarian/vegan available); the official site confirms the guesthouse/café/rental setup and book-trade coffee.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Travel coverage states that vegetarian and vegan guests can be accommodated for the tea-rice set, indicating the kitchen is willing to adjust, but no formal allergy/cross-contact protocol is published.

positives.text: The core meal is a simple, rice-and-vegetable homestyle set with miso soup and Nara pickles, and the egg is an optional add-on, making it easy to keep the plate plant-based on request.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a quiet, intimate family-run machiya with just a few seats, so a little Japanese (or a translation app) helps; the owner is welcoming to travelers, but it has a homey "grandmother's house" feel rather than a tourist-restaurant setup.

nara_rokkan_room.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The signature nyūmen is made with Miwa sōmen (wheat noodles), and the menu features curries and a custard pudding. No gluten-free menu, dedicated preparation, or celiac accommodations are documented; broths almost certainly contain wheat-based seasonings and the place is not set up for cross-contamination control.
nara_rokkan_room.vegan_detail: Not a vegan venue. Some dishes appear plant-leaning (spiced fried-tofu nyūmen, chai-infused red-bean zenzai), but nyūmen broth is typically made with fish dashi and curries are not confirmed animal-free; the pudding uses Nara eggs. A flexible vegetarian might find an item by asking, but vegans should not assume any dish is safe without confirming dashi and curry ingredients.

chef_bio.background: ROKKAN ROOM occupies a townhouse more than 140 years old in Motobayashiin-cho, once the heart of Nara's old flower district just south of Sarusawa Pond. The building was formerly an okiya (a residence for geisha), and owner Moe Oyagi actually lived in it before reimagining it as a café. She kept the layers of its past intact: the original earthen-floored entry, a storehouse (kura), repurposed lacquer tables from the okiya, and a wartime air-raid shelter in the basement now softened with tatami and cushions.
chef_bio.philosophy: Cooking around the themes of fermentation and spice using local Nara ingredients, herbs and medicinal touches, while preserving and celebrating the building's many historical layers through a deliberately eclectic old-meets-new design.
chef_bio.specialty: Nyūmen made with Nara's local Miwa sōmen, served with a spiced fried-tofu pouch that releases curry when broken open; a chai-infused zenzai (red-bean soup) layering cinnamon, ginger and clove over strained sweet beans; and a custard pudding made with Nara-prefecture eggs.

anecdotes.text: The basement, a former air-raid shelter, has low ceilings and bare concrete walls but is laid with tatami and plush cushions, with speakers playing hypersonic sound to help guests relax in a space that feels cut off from the modern world.
A second-floor gallery room displays works by knit artist Chihiro Hasunuma and features a round table that converts to a kotatsu in winter.
The chai-tea zenzai was born from one of the owner's inspirations: the aroma reads as chai, the first sip tastes like zenzai, and the finish returns to chai.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Co-trip confirms owner Moe Oyagi, the 140+yr former okiya she once lived in near Sarusawa Pond, the preserved earthen entry, kura and lacquered okiya tables, the basement air-raid-shelter room with tatami/cushions/hypersonic sound, the Miwa-somen nyumen with a curry-filled tofu pouch, the chai zenzai, the Nara-egg pudding, and the Hasunuma knit-art gallery with a kotatsu-convertible round table.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Signature nyūmen uses Miwa sōmen (wheat noodles) and the menu includes curries, so wheat is central to the kitchen; no gluten-free preparation or separation is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Nyūmen broth is typically fish-based and the custard pudding uses eggs; no vegan menu or animal-free assurances were found.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed, art-filled café where a warm greeting in Japanese goes a long way; staff may not speak much English, so a translation app helps for asking about ingredients.

nara_tabi_coffee_roaster.gf_detail: A specialty coffee stand, not a gluten-free destination. The only food offered is the owner's wife's homemade baked goods (canelé, biscotti), which are wheat-based. No gluten-free items or celiac handling are documented. Coffee itself is naturally gluten-free, but there is no dedicated GF preparation.
nara_tabi_coffee_roaster.vegan_detail: This is primarily a coffee stand. Black coffee is plant-based, but milk-based drinks use dairy and no plant-milk option is documented. The accompanying baked goods (canelé, biscotti) typically contain eggs and dairy. No vegan menu or labeling exists; a vegan visitor would need to stick to black coffee and ask about any food.
nara_tabi_coffee_roaster.hours_raw: Tabelog: weekdays 12:00-18:00 / holidays 12:00-17:00. Closed Wed, 1st and 3rd Sun, plus irregular days off. (Another source, Narakko, lists 9:30-19:00, until 18:00 Sun/holidays, so hours vary.)

chef_bio.background: TABI Coffee Roaster opened on July 18, 2017, tucked inside the retro Tsubai Market (椿井市場) arcade a short walk from Kintetsu Nara Station. The owner spent roughly 11-13 years training as a roaster at the well-known Nara coffee house Kuroko before striking out on his own, and he runs the stand together with his wife, who hand-bakes the pastries.
chef_bio.philosophy: A focus on careful, small-batch hand-roasting using fully hand-picked premium beans, aiming to make fresh, approachable coffee that appeals to a wide range of ages.
chef_bio.specialty: House-roasted single-origin and blend coffees, including the signature TABI Blend (a deeper roast with pronounced bitterness and depth) and a medium-roast version, plus rotating single origins. The shop is small-batch and hands-on: the owner hand-picks world-class green beans to remove defects, then roasts in small lots from medium to dark. His wife's homemade canelé and biscotti accompany the coffee.

anecdotes.text: The owner hand-picks the world-class green beans to remove poor beans before roasting them in small lots across medium to deep roasts.

The shop is hidden inside a retro market arcade, standing out for its simple glass-sliding-door look among the surrounding old vendors; the owner's wife bakes the canelé and biscotti served alongside the coffee.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Nara-gourmet and narakko confirm the Tsubai-cho market location, the owner's ~11-13-year roasting career at Kuroko (now cafe CROCO), hand-picked small-batch medium-to-deep roasting, the TABI Blend, and the wife's canele/biscotti; a web search confirms the July 18, 2017 opening. The owner's personal name is not published.

positives.text: Black drip and single-origin coffees are the core offering and are naturally free of gluten and animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, friendly owner-run coffee stand in a retro market arcade; a few words of Japanese and a smile go a long way, though ordering coffee is simple and approachable for a foreign student.

nara_wanzu_heart_cafe_naramac.gf_detail: Not gluten-free friendly. Signature items include fried shrimp and chicken (wheat batter) and a kudzu-udon pasta dish; an official allergen note for the lunch lists shrimp, wheat and eggs. Soy sauce and miso here are standard wheat-containing types, so it is not safe for celiacs.
nara_wanzu_heart_cafe_naramac.vegan_detail: This is a homestyle Japanese cafe whose signature plates feature fried chicken, fried shrimp, fish, miso soup and egg-based items. No vegan menu is documented and dishes rely on standard Japanese seasonings and likely fish dashi, so it is not a vegan destination.
nara_wanzu_heart_cafe_naramac.hours_raw: Mon, Tue, Thu, Fri, Sat & holidays 9:00-17:00 (food L.O. 16:00, drink L.O. 16:30); Sun 9:00-19:00/20:00 (food L.O. 18:00/19:00). Closed Wednesdays. Evening dining available by phone consultation.
